narrative:
The model predicted a 63% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was denied.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your class ranking in your third year of law school was the strongest influence, and it pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. You placed in the bottom decile (1 out of 10), far below the average of roughly the middle of the class among students who were accepted. Your first-year ranking also mattered, though less so; finishing in the third decile rather than the sixth-decile average pulled the prediction slightly in a more favorable direction, but not enough to offset the later performance.

Your LSAT score was the second most important factor and worked against you. A score of 22 is well below the average of 37 seen among accepted applicants, and this gap significantly increased the model’s estimate of bar exam failure.

Taken together, these academic signals led the model to conclude that the risk of failing the bar was too high for admission. 

What you should do next is focus on improving your academic performance and retaking the LSAT. Raising both your class standing and test score in the coming months would substantially improve your chances in a future application.
